entry.gloss: the beat split into two or three equal parts
entry.def: The first level of equal parts into which a beat is split: two in simple meter (eighth notes under a quarter-note beat) and three in compound meter (eighth notes under a dotted quarter-note beat).

figure.staff: B4/q B4/q | B4/e B4/e B4/e B4/e |.

entry.gloss: the beat's divisions split again
entry.def: The next level below the beat division: each part of the division split into two, such as sixteenth notes under a quarter-note or dotted quarter-note beat. Counting the subdivision helps to place short notes and dotted rhythms exactly.

figure.staff: B4/q. B4/q. | B4/e B4/e B4/e B4/e B4/e B4/e | B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s B4/s |.
figure.caption: In 6/8: the beats, their division into eighth notes and the subdivision into sixteenth notes.

entry.gloss: two dotted beats in a bar, as in 6/8
entry.def: A compound meter with two beats in each bar, each a dotted note divided into three: 6/8 (two dotted quarter notes), and also 6/4 and 6/16. Called compound duple time in British English.

figure.staff: C5/q E5/e G5/q E5/e | F5/e E5/e D5/e C5/q. |.

entry.gloss: three dotted beats in a bar, as in 9/8
entry.def: A compound meter with three beats in each bar, each a dotted note divided into three: 9/8 (three dotted quarter notes), and also 9/4 and 9/16. Called compound triple time in British English.

figure.staff: C5/q E5/e D5/q F5/e E5/q G5/e | C6/q. G5/q. C5/q. |.

entry.gloss: four dotted beats in a bar, as in 12/8
entry.def: A compound meter with four beats in each bar, each a dotted note divided into three: 12/8 (four dotted quarter notes), and also 12/4 and 12/16. Called compound quadruple time in British English.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/e F5/q D5/e E5/q. C5/q. | G4/w. |.

entry.gloss: irregular group in the time of a regular one
entry.def: A group of notes played in the time of a different number of the same value, marked with a number and often a bracket: a triplet (three in the time of two), a duplet (two in the time of three), or a quintuplet (five in the time of four).

figure.caption: Five sixteenth notes in the time of four.

entry.gloss: three notes in the time of two
entry.def: A tuplet of three equal notes in the time of two of the same value, marked 3: three triplet eighth notes fill a quarter note, and three triplet quarter notes a half note. Triplets borrow the division of compound meter in simple meter.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/e3 F5/e3 G5/e3 | A5/q G5/q |.

entry.gloss: two notes in the time of three
entry.def: A tuplet of two equal notes in the time of three of the same value, marked 2: in 6/8, two duplet eighth notes fill a dotted quarter-note beat. Duplets borrow the division of simple meter in compound meter, and are sometimes written as two dotted eighth notes instead.

figure.staff: C5/e D5/e E5/e F5/e2 G5/e2 | A5/q. G5/q. |.

entry.gloss: long–short pattern made with a dotted note
entry.def: A rhythm in which a dotted note is followed by a short note that completes the beat or beat pair, such as a dotted eighth and a sixteenth, or a dotted quarter and an eighth. In Baroque French overtures such rhythms were often played sharper than written.

figure.staff: C5/q. D5/e E5/q. F5/e | G5/e. A5/s G5/e. F5/s E5/h |.

entry.gloss: adds half and then a quarter of the value
entry.def: Two dots after a note or rest, which add half its value and then a quarter of its value: a double-dotted half note lasts seven eighth notes, and a double-dotted quarter note seven sixteenth notes. The short note that follows usually completes the beat.

entry.gloss: short–long pattern on the beat
entry.def: A short note on the beat followed by a longer dotted note, the reverse of the usual dotted rhythm: a sixteenth and a dotted eighth. Also called the Scotch snap, after its use in Scottish folk music.

entry.gloss: three twos in the place of two threes
entry.def: A rhythm that puts three groups of two beats in the place of two groups of three, so that two bars of 3/4 sound like one bar of 3/2. It is common at cadences in Baroque music. The name comes from the Greek for one and a half, the ratio 3:2.

figure.staff: C5/q D5/q E5/q | F5/h E5/q~ | E5/q D5/h | C5/h. |.
figure.caption: In the second and third bars the stresses fall every two beats.

entry.gloss: shortest recognizable musical idea
entry.def: A short rhythmic or melodic idea, often only a few notes long, that is repeated and developed through a piece. Spelled motif in British English.

figure.staff: r/e G4/e G4/e G4/e | Eb4/h | r/e F4/e F4/e F4/e | D4/h |.
figure.caption: The opening motive of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony, stated and then repeated a step lower.

entry.gloss: musical unit that ends with a cadence
entry.def: A complete musical thought that ends with a cadence, often four bars long. This is the definition of Kostka and Payne and most American textbooks; Caplin uses phrase more loosely for a unit of about four bars, whether or not it ends with a cadence.

entry.gloss: two phrases: a question and its answer
entry.def: Two phrases heard as a pair, an antecedent ending with a weaker cadence and a consequent ending with a stronger one, typically a half cadence answered by a perfect authentic cadence.

figure.staff: C4/q C4/q D4/q E4/q | E4/q. D4/e D4/h || C4/q C4/q D4/q E4/q | D4/q. C4/e C4/h |.
figure.caption: The ends of the two phrases of the Ode to Joy from Beethoven's Ninth Symphony: the first stops on the second degree over a half cadence, the second closes on the tonic.

entry.gloss: first phrase of a period, with the weaker cadence
entry.def: The first phrase of a period, which ends with a weak cadence, usually a half cadence and sometimes an imperfect authentic cadence, so that it sounds like a question.

entry.gloss: second phrase of a period, with the stronger cadence
entry.def: The second phrase of a period, which answers the antecedent with a stronger cadence, usually a perfect authentic cadence.

entry.gloss: period whose two phrases begin alike
entry.def: A period whose consequent begins with the same or similar melodic material as the antecedent, as in the Ode to Joy.

entry.gloss: period whose two phrases begin differently
entry.def: A period whose consequent begins with different melodic material from the antecedent; the cadences alone make the two phrases a pair.

entry.gloss: four phrases in two period-like halves
entry.def: Four phrases grouped like a period in which each half has two phrases: the second phrase ends with a weak cadence, usually a half cadence, and the fourth with a stronger one, usually a perfect authentic cadence.

entry.gloss: idea, its repetition, then continuation to a cadence
entry.def: A theme type, usually eight bars, made of a presentation, a two-bar basic idea and its repetition, followed by a continuation that breaks the idea into smaller pieces and drives to a cadence. The term comes from Schoenberg and was developed by Caplin.

entry.gloss: first half of a sentence: the idea stated twice
entry.def: The first part of a sentence: a basic idea and its repetition, exact or on another degree, over a tonic harmony. It does not end with a cadence.

entry.gloss: second half of a sentence, breaking up the idea
entry.def: The second part of a sentence, which destabilizes the presentation through fragmentation, faster harmonic rhythm and often sequences, and ends with a cadence.

entry.gloss: two-bar opening idea of a theme
entry.def: In Caplin's theory, the idea of about two bars, usually made of several motives, that begins a sentence or a period.

entry.gloss: breaking an idea into shorter units
entry.def: Shortening the units in which material is grouped, for example from two-bar to one-bar ideas, typically in the continuation of a sentence.

entry.gloss: a phrase lengthened beyond its expected size
entry.def: Lengthening a phrase beyond its expected length, often four bars, by repeating or delaying the cadence, inserting extra material in the middle, or adding a short introduction. Also called phrase expansion.

entry.gloss: one phrase's last bar is the next one's first
entry.def: The overlapping of two phrases so that the cadence of the first and the beginning of the second fall on the same beat: the bar that ends one phrase also begins the next.
